summary: Micah 1 opens by locating the prophet in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah and by naming Samaria and Jerusalem as the concern of the vision. The chapter then summons the peoples and the earth to hear as Yahweh comes in judgment, naming Samaria and Jerusalem as centers of disobedience. It ends in a public lament that moves through towns of Judah, with grief reaching the gate of Jerusalem and exile named as the final wound.
whyItMatters: This chapter sets the book’s opening pattern: public accusation, announced judgment, and grief for communities caught in disaster. It also ties Samaria, Jerusalem, and Judah’s countryside together, so the reader should not hear the book as only a private message to one city.

context.author: The heading attributes the word to Micah of Morasheth; it does not identify everyone involved in arranging the finished book.
context.audience: The chapter addresses peoples and the earth, then speaks concerning Samaria, Jerusalem, and towns of Judah.
context.date: The heading places Micah in the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, an eighth-century BCE setting; the date of the finished book is not supplied.
context.setting: The concerns center on Samaria, Jerusalem, and the Judean countryside southwest of Jerusalem, in a period when Assyrian pressure forms part of the historical horizon.
context.literaryForm: Prophetic heading, summons, judgment speech, and lament, with rapid movement from cosmic imagery to named towns.

outline.heading: The prophet and the cities named
outline.note: The opening identifies Micah of Morasheth, the Judean kings in whose days the word came, and the subject as Samaria and Jerusalem.

outline.heading: The earth summoned to hear
outline.note: Peoples and the earth are told to hear while Yahweh is pictured coming down, with mountains melting and valleys splitting before him.

outline.heading: Samaria and Jerusalem accused
outline.note: The chapter names the disobedience of Jacob and the sins of Israel, then announces Samaria’s ruin and the destruction of its idols and images.

outline.heading: The lament reaches Jerusalem
outline.note: A first-person voice laments, wails, and mourns because the wound has reached Judah and the gate of Jerusalem.

outline.heading: Town-by-town lament
outline.note: The lament moves through Gath, Beth Ophrah, Shaphir, Zaanan, Beth Ezel, Maroth, Lachish, Moresheth Gath, Achzib, Mareshah, and Adullam, describing shame, anxiety, parting, deceit, and conquest.

outline.heading: Mourning for children taken away
outline.note: The closing command tells the hearers to shave their heads in grief because beloved children have gone into captivity.

keyVerses.text: Hear, you peoples, all of you! Listen, O earth, and all that is therein. Let the Lord Yahweh be witness against you, the Lord from his holy temple.
keyVerses.why: This verse makes the chapter public and formal: the audience is wider than one city, and Yahweh is named as witness.

keyVerses.text: “All this is for the disobedience of Jacob, and for the sins of the house of Israel. What is the disobedience of Jacob? Isn’t it Samaria? And what are the high places of Judah? Aren’t they Jerusalem?
keyVerses.why: The verse gives the stated reason for the upheaval and names Samaria and Jerusalem as central to the accusation.

keyVerses.text: For her wounds are incurable; for it has come even to Judah. It reaches to the gate of my people, even to Jerusalem.
keyVerses.why: This verse marks the movement from Samaria’s ruin toward Judah and Jerusalem, which drives the lament that follows.

keyVerses.text: Shave your heads, and cut off your hair for the children of your delight. Enlarge your baldness like the vulture, for they have gone into captivity from you!
keyVerses.why: The last verse closes the chapter in mourning and names captivity as the outcome for the children addressed.

questions.question: Who is Micah of Morasheth?
questions.answer: Verse 1 names Micah of Morasheth as the person to whom Yahweh’s word came. Moresheth lay in the Judean countryside southwest of Jerusalem. The heading gives his name, place association, and the kings during whose days he saw the word concerning Samaria and Jerusalem, without providing a full biography.

questions.question: Why does the chapter begin with Samaria and Jerusalem?
questions.answer: Verse 1 says the vision concerns Samaria and Jerusalem, and verse 5 names both cities while speaking of disobedience and sins. The chapter does not treat the problem as only local to one town; its opening accusation involves the leading cities of Israel and Judah.

questions.question: What does “Hear” signal at the start of the speech?
questions.answer: In verse 2, “Hear” is a summons to attention for “you peoples” and for the earth and all within it. The verse frames what follows as public testimony, with the Lord Yahweh described as witness from his holy temple.

questions.question: Are the melting mountains and split valleys meant as a map of an event?
questions.answer: Verses 3-4 use large poetic images for Yahweh’s coming: high places are tread on, mountains melt, and valleys split like wax before fire or water poured down a steep place. The chapter’s own point is the overwhelming force of Yahweh’s arrival, not a detailed physical map.

questions.question: What happens to Samaria in this chapter?
questions.answer: Verse 6 says Samaria will become like a rubble heap of the field and places for planting vineyards, with its stones poured into the valley and its foundations uncovered. Verse 7 adds that idols, temple gifts, and images will be destroyed, so the judgment includes both the city’s structure and its objects of worship.

questions.question: Why does the speaker lament so intensely?
questions.answer: Verse 8 says, “For this I will lament and wail,” and describes stripped, naked mourning with animal-like cries. Verse 9 gives the reason: the wounds are called incurable, and the disaster has come to Judah and reaches the gate of Jerusalem.

questions.question: Why are so many town names listed in verses 10-15?
questions.answer: The lament moves through named places, turning judgment into a town-by-town grief rather than an abstract warning. Hebrew soundplay links some names with the disaster described: Achzib echoes a word for disappointment, while Beth Ophrah is paired with rolling in dust. English retains the movement through shame, anxiety, loss, and conquest, even where the sound links are lost. Not every town can be located with certainty.

questions.question: What is difficult about Lachish being called “the beginning of sin”?
questions.answer: Verse 13 addresses Lachish and says, “She was the beginning of sin to the daughter of Zion,” because the transgressions of Israel were found there. The chapter does not explain exactly how Lachish contributed to that wrongdoing. It places the town within the spread of guilt and danger named in the lament.

questions.question: What does shaving the head mean at the end?
questions.answer: Verse 16 commands shaved heads and enlarged baldness as an act of mourning for “the children of your delight.” The reason given is captivity: “they have gone into captivity from you,” so the physical sign matches a communal loss.

glossary.def: The place associated with Micah in verse 1, in the Judean countryside southwest of Jerusalem.
One of the two cities named in verse 1 as the subject of the vision and in verse 5 as tied to the disobedience of Jacob.
The place from which verse 2 says the Lord is witness; the phrase belongs to the chapter’s public summons and witness scene.
A phrase used in verse 3 for places Yahweh treads on and in verse 5 when Jerusalem is named in connection with Judah.
The condition named in verse 16 for the children who have gone away, prompting the command to mourn.
